t.6.61.1: When those two had been struck down at the forefront of battle, the army of the monkey troop-leaders was thrown into bewilderment, and Sugrīva, Nīla, Aṅgada and Jāmbavān could not grasp anything at all.
t.6.61.2: Then Vibhīṣaṇa, foremost among the wise, seeing the army dejected, spoke to the heroic lords of the monkeys, reassuring them with incomparable words.
t.6.61.3: Do not be afraid; this is no time for despair, though the two noble princes lie helpless and dejected. It is in upholding the word of Svayambhū that they have been laid low by Indrajit's nets of missiles.
t.6.61.5: Then the wise Hanūmān, son of Māruta, having honored the Brahmā weapon and having heard the words of Vibhīṣaṇa, spoke to him.
t.6.61.4: This supreme Brahmā weapon of unfailing force was given to him by Svayambhū. If the two princes have fallen out of respect for it, what occasion is there here for despair?
t.6.61.6: Now that this army of the mighty vānaras has been struck down, let the two of us comfort each and every one who still holds on to life.
t.6.61.7: Then, in the night, those two heroes, Hanumān and the foremost of the rākṣasas, moved together across the front of the battlefield with torches in their hands.
t.6.61.8: With tails, hands, thighs, feet, fingers and necks severed, and with limbs oozing blood and streaming with it on every side.
t.6.61.9: The two of them beheld the earth crowded with fallen monkeys, huge as mountains, and strewn with fallen, gleaming weapons.
t.6.61.11: Vibhīṣaṇa and Hanumān saw Mainda, Nala, Jyotirmukha, Dvivida and Panasa as well, struck down on the battlefield.
t.6.61.10: Sugrīva, Aṅgada, Nīla, Śarabha, Gandhamādana, Jāmbavant and Suṣeṇa, Vegadarśana and Āhuka.
t.6.61.13: Seeing the army, formidable and like the surging flood of the ocean, tormented by arrows, Hanūmān together with Vibhīṣaṇa went in search of Jāmbavant.
t.6.61.12: Sixty-seven crores of swift monkeys have been slain by the favourite of Svayambhū in the remaining fifth part of the day.
t.6.61.14: Him, the aged hero, son of Prajāpati, burdened with the natural decay of old age and covered with hundreds of arrows, like a fire that is dying down.
t.6.61.15: Seeing him, Paulastya approached and spoke these words: "Noble one, I trust your life-breaths have not been destroyed by the sharp arrows?"
t.6.61.16: Having heard Vibhīṣaṇa's words, Jāmbavān, the bull among bears, uttering his speech with difficulty, spoke these words.
t.6.61.17: By your voice, that of the mighty lord of the Nairṛtas, I recognize you; tormented by sharp arrows, I cannot see you with my eyes.
t.6.61.19: Having heard the words of Jāmbavant, Vibhīṣaṇa said this: "Passing over the two noble princes, why do you ask about Māruti?"
t.6.61.18: O Nairṛta, is Hanumān, the best of the vānaras, through whom Añjanā and Mātariśvan are blessed with a worthy son, still holding on to his life somewhere?
t.6.61.20: O noble one, not toward King Sugrīva, nor toward Aṅgada, nor even toward Rāghava have you shown such supreme affection as you have toward the son of Vāyu.
t.6.61.22: As long as that hero lives, our army, though slain, is not slain; but should Hanūmān give up his life, then even though we live, we are slain.
t.6.61.21: Having heard Vibhīṣaṇa's words, Jāmbavān spoke: "Listen, O tiger among the Nairṛtas, to why I ask about Māruti."
t.6.61.23: Dear one, if Māruti, who is like Māruta and equal to Vaiśvānara in valour, still lives, then there may be hope of life.
t.6.61.24: Then Hanūmān, son of the Wind-god, approached the aged Jāmbavān and, clasping his feet, saluted him with due observance.
t.6.61.26: Then the greatly radiant Jāmbavān said to Hanūmān: "Come, O tiger among monkeys! You must save the vānaras."
t.6.61.25: Hearing Hanumān's words, the bull among bears, though his senses were still afflicted, regarded himself as if born again.
t.6.61.27: No one else is equal to this feat of valour; you are their supreme friend. This is the hour for your prowess; I see no one else at all.
t.6.61.28: Gladden the hosts of the heroic bears and monkeys, and make these two, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, who have been struck down, free of their arrow-wounds.
t.6.61.29: O Hanūmān, having travelled a great distance high above the ocean, you should go to Himavant, the best of mountains.
t.6.61.30: Then, O destroyer of foes, you will see the golden and exceedingly formidable Ṛṣabha, the best of mountains, and also the peak of Kailāsa.
t.6.61.31: Between those two peaks, O hero, you will see the Mountain of Herbs, blazing, of incomparable splendor, and filled with every kind of herb.
t.6.61.32: O tiger among monkeys, on its summit you will see four herbs growing, blazing and lighting up the ten directions.
t.6.61.33: Bring the Mṛtasaṃjīvanī, which restores the dead to life, and the Viśalyakaraṇī, which draws out arrows and heals wounds, as well as the Sauvarṇakaraṇī, which restores the body's golden hue, and the Saṃdhānī, the great herb that knits together broken limbs.
t.6.61.35: Having heard the words of Jāmbavant, Hanūmān, bull among the monkeys, was filled with surges of strength and exultation, as the ocean is filled by the rushing force of its waters.
t.6.61.34: Taking all of them, O Hanumān, you should come back swiftly; then, son of the Wind, restore the monkeys to their life-breaths and revive them.
t.6.61.36: Standing upon the summit of the mountain's slope and pressing down upon that foremost of mountains, the heroic Hanūmān appeared like a second mountain.
t.6.61.37: Split apart by the monkey's feet, that mountain sank down; severely crushed, it could not bear itself up.
t.6.61.38: As the mountain was pressed by Hanumān, its trees fell to the ground and blazed from the monkey's force, and its peaks were scattered.
t.6.61.39: As that excellent mountain was being pressed down, its surface strewn with shattered trees and rocks, and as it reeled and shook, the monkeys were unable to keep their footing.
t.6.61.40: Then that Laṅkā, its great gates swaying and its houses and gate-towers shattered, stricken with terror in the night, seemed as if it were dancing.
t.6.61.41: Resembling a mountain himself, the son of Māruta pressed down upon the mountain and made the earth, together with its oceans, tremble.
t.6.61.42: Pressing down the mountain with his two feet and opening wide his fierce mouth like the mare-faced fire beneath the ocean, he roared loudly, as if to terrify the rākṣasas.
t.6.61.43: Hearing the wondrous roar of him as he bellowed again and again, all the rākṣasas dwelling in Laṅkā were unable to stir from fear.
t.6.61.44: Then, having bowed to Rāma, Māruti of terrible prowess, the scorcher of foes, set his mind on a supreme deed for the sake of Rāghava.
t.6.61.45: Raising his serpent-like tail, bending his back and folding down his ears, and opening wide his mouth like the fiery Vaḍavāmukha, he of fierce speed leapt up into the sky.
t.6.61.46: With his might he swept along clumps of trees, hills, rocks and ordinary monkeys; tossed up and hurled forward by the rushing force of his arms and thighs, they fell into the water once their momentum was spent.
t.6.61.47: Stretching out his two arms, which were like the coils of serpents, the son of Vāyu, whose might equalled that of Garuḍa, the foe of serpents, went toward Meru, the foremost king of mountains, as though dragging the directions along with him.
t.6.61.48: Gazing then upon the ocean, its garlands of waves tossing and all its creatures violently whirled about, he sped onward swiftly, like the discus hurled from the tip of Viṣṇu's hand.
t.6.61.50: Taking to the path of the sun, he went on, free from weariness. That foremost of monkeys beheld Himavant, the greatest of mountains.
t.6.61.49: He, whose speed equalled his father's, sped swiftly onward, beholding mountains, clusters of trees, lakes, rivers, ponds and excellent cities, and those flourishing Añjanas as well.
t.6.61.51: It was endowed with many springs, full of caves and waterfalls, and adorned with lovely peaks resembling masses of white clouds.
t.6.61.52: Having reached that great lord of mountains, whose lofty, excellent and terrible peaks rose exceedingly high, he beheld holy great hermitages frequented by the foremost hosts of gods and seers.
t.6.61.53: He beheld the Brahmakośa, the silver abode, the abode of Śakra, the place where Rudra released his arrow, Hayānana, the blazing Brahmaśiras, and the servants of Vaivasvata.
t.6.61.55: He beheld the foremost Kailāsa and the rock of Himavat, and likewise Ṛṣabha, the foremost golden mountain, and the lord of mountains bearing all herbs, ablaze with all its shining herbs.
t.6.61.54: He saw the abode of the thunderbolt and the abode of Vaiśravaṇa, the place radiant as the sun and the place where the sun is bound, the seat of Brahmā, the bow of Śaṃkara, and the navel of the earth.
t.6.61.56: Beholding that mountain blazing with rays like fire, the son of Vāsava's messenger was astonished; and leaping onto that lord of herb-bearing mountains, he began a search for the herbs there.
t.6.61.57: Having crossed thousands of yojanas, that great monkey, the son of Māruta, roamed over the mountain that bears the divine herbs.
t.6.61.58: But all those great medicinal herbs on that best of mountains, perceiving that a seeker was approaching, then vanished from sight.
t.6.61.59: Not seeing them, the great-souled Hanumān grew angry and, in his wrath, roared loudly. Unable to bear it, his eyes blazing like fire, he spoke these words to that lord of mountains.
t.6.61.60: Is this, then, so firmly resolved by you, that you show no compassion toward Rāghava? Behold yourself today, O lord of mountains, overpowered by the strength of my arms and scattered to pieces.
t.6.61.61: He seized its peak, with its trees, its elephants and its gold, rich with thousands of minerals, its crags scattered and its upper slopes shaken, and with a mighty rush he suddenly tore it away.
t.6.61.63: Having entered upon the path of the sun, and holding that peak which shone like the sun, he then appeared like the sun itself, shining near Ravi as a second sun.
t.6.61.62: Having uprooted it, he flew up into the sky, terrifying the worlds together with the gods and the lords of the gods; and, praised by many sky-ranging beings, he whose valor was as fierce as Garuḍa's sped onward with great swiftness.
t.6.61.64: And that son of the Wind-god, himself like a mountain, shone exceedingly with that mountain, like Viṣṇu in the sky with his thousand-edged discus, blazing with fire, held aloft.
t.6.61.65: Seeing him, the monkeys then roared, and he too, seeing them, roared with joy. Hearing the loud uproar they raised, the dwellers of Laṅkā roared still more terribly.
t.6.61.66: Then the great-souled one descended upon that foremost of mountains in the midst of the monkey army. Bowing his head in salutation to the foremost of the monkeys, he there embraced Vibhīṣaṇa.
t.6.61.67: Those two princes of men, too, having inhaled the fragrance of the great healing herbs, became free of their arrow-wounds there at that time, and the other foremost heroes among the monkeys rose up as well.
t.6.61.68: Then the monkey, the son of the Wind, of towering might, swiftly carried that mountain of herbs back to Himavant itself, and once more he rejoined Rāma.
